preamble: Affrication and lateralization of /t/ to the lateral affricate [tɬ] is the sound law known as Whorf's law: in Proto-Nahuan (Proto-Aztecan), Proto-Uto-Aztecan *t became *tɬ before *a (and, per Manaster Ramer 1996, before the high central vowel *ɨ). It is the source of the famous Nahuatl /tɬ/, including the absolutive suffix -tl < *-ta. The conditioning vowel was often later lost or changed, obscuring the environment, and some Nahuan varieties (e.g. Pipil, eastern dialects) later reverted /tɬ/ to /t/ or shifted it to /l/. Outside Nahuan the change is essentially unknown, so it is cross-linguistically rare.

examples.note: Via Proto-Nahuan *tlaaka-tl; both the initial *t and the absolutive suffix *-ta show *t > tɬ before *a.
Via Proto-Nahuan *tai(h)-tl; the conditioning *a was later changed, but tɬ remains. Compare non-Nahuan cognates with plain t: Yaqui taji, Cora taíj, Huichol tái.

sources: Whorf, B. L. (1937). The Origin of Aztec TL. American Anthropologist 39(2), 265-274. https://doi.org/10.1525/aa.1937.39.2.02a00070
Campbell, L., & Langacker, R. W. (1978). Proto-Aztecan Vowels: Part I. International Journal of American Linguistics 44(2), 85-102. https://doi.org/10.1086/465526
